transcript:
Meeting header:
Date/Time: 2025-10-02 15:00 UTC
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Alex Rivera (Redwood AE), Maya Patel (Redwood SE), Jordan Kim (Redwood Solutions), Dr. Lian Chen (CTO, AsterBio), Ravi Desai (Head of ML), Sofia Morales (Lead Infra)

--- Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be partial) ---
Redwood walked through latency/throughput tradeoffs for embedding-based rerank pipelines. Discussed sample workloads, current vector dims (384/768), batch sizing, and opportunities for KV cache to short-circuit expensive calls. Quantization (8-bit vs 4-bit) came up as a cost lever with potential accuracy impact. AsterBio concerned about VPC egress and on-prem network constraints. Action: Redwood to run 10k rerank benchmark and produce cost/latency matrix.

[00:00] Alex (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining — I think we have about 50 minutes. Quick roll call?
[00:06] Dr. Chen (AsterBio): Lian here — hi.
[00:08] Ravi (AsterBio): Ravi — hey.
[00:10] Sofia (AsterBio): Sofia here.
[00:12] Maya (Redwood SE): Maya on the call. Jordan too.
[00:15] Alex: Cool, thanks. We're here to zoom into embeddings rerank perf and cost — Jordan and Maya will drive the tech bits.

[02:05] Maya: Quick baseline: from our prep you mentioned two main pipelines — immediate top-N retrieval using FAISS then an online rerank step that scores the top 100 with a cross-encoder (or bi-encoder + dot). Can you confirm typical top-K and SLA?
[02:22] Ravi: Yeah, we do top-200 recall at retrieval then rerank 50-100. SLA is 200ms p95 for rerank-only path; full search end-to-end 350ms p95.
[02:40] Maya: Helpful. What's your vector dims now?
[02:42] Ravi: Primary product uses 768 dim embeddings for semantic search, but we have legacy 384 for an older index. Most traffic is 768.
[02:50] Maya: Got it. That helps frame throughput.

[05:00] Jordan: Two quick knobs: batch size (how many queries you send in single inference call) and vector dim (affects FLOPs). Also KV-cache where prefix context or repeated pieces can be cached. For embeddings rerank specifically, caching isn't as straightforward as autoregressive generation but we can cache candidate encodes or cross-encoder outputs for repeated queries.
[05:25] Sofia: Can you clarify KV-cache in this context? I thought KV cache was mostly for decoder cache.
[05:33] Maya: Good point — we used "kay V cache" a bit loosely. For rerank, think of two caches — an index-level cache (document embeddings cached in memory) and an inference-level cache (cross-encoder outputs or partial inner-product results). The latter is more like a result cache keyed on query fingerprint. It's not the GPT-style KV cache, so apologies for wording confusion — sometimes our notes say "kay V cache" in the transcript.
[06:05] Ravi: Right, so we can cache the expensive cross-encoder only for highly repeat queries. But our query distribution is long-tail.

[07:02] Maya: Exactly — hit-rate is critical. If hit-rate < 5-10% the cache won't move the needle. We asked for sample query frequency earlier; Sofia can you confirm heavy repeat percent?
[07:18] Sofia: In our logs about 18% of queries are identical within a 24h window; another 10% are near-duplicates. So with some fingerprint grouping maybe we get to 25% effective hit-rate.
[07:30] Alex: That's promising. At 25% hit-rate, cost savings compound because rerank is the heavy op.

[09:00] Maya: Next: batch sizing. For embedding/rerank workloads we typically see an efficiency sweet spot per GPU: too small batches increase per-token overhead, too big batches push latency. For your SLO (200ms p95) we recommend batching 8-32 for cross-encoder depending on model size.
[09:22] Ravi: Is that 8-32 per GPU? We run multi-tenant pods.
[09:26] Jordan: Per inference shard — yes. If you have N replicas the effective concurrency multiplies. Also, batching on the client side vs server side matters; Redwood's runtime can do continuous batching which helps keep tail latency down.
[09:40] Ravi: Does continuous batching risk increasing p95 in bursts?
[09:44] Maya: It can if your batching policy waits too long. We use adaptive max-wait timers: e.g., 8ms max-wait for low-latency tiers. That usually keeps p95 within SLO while improving throughput by 1.8–3x depending on model.

[11:50] Sofia: On quantization — you mentioned 8-bit and 4-bit. How stable are accuracy numbers for rerank if we go to 8-bit or 4-bit?
[12:02] Maya: For most cross-encoders, 8-bit quant gives negligible rank-order impact (<1% nDCG delta), 4-bit can introduce more variance; it depends on model family. We recommend running evals on your held-out rerank labels. For vector dims, if you reduce from 768->384 you drop recall on certain queries but throughput roughly halves and cost per query drops similarly.
[12:30] Ravi: Is quantization applied to both embedding generation and cross-encoder?
[12:34] Maya: Typically embeddings (bi-encoders) are safe at 8-bit and sometimes 4-bit with PQ/OPQ compression; cross-encoders are more sensitive but 8-bit is common. Also consider mixed precision: keep the last layer in fp16.

[14:00] Alex: Let's ground this with numbers — suppose a baseline cross-encoder at 768 dims, FP16, batching=1 gives 120ms median and 260ms p95 on a single A100-like GPU for 100-rerank calls. If we do batching=16 and continuous batching we push throughput x6 and p95 to ~200ms. Quant to 8-bit may get another 1.5x. These are approximate — subject to model kernel support.
[14:35] Ravi: Those are useful. How does vector dimension factor into that latency?
[14:40] Maya: Vector dim affects both memory bandwidth and compute. Going 768->384 reduces multiply-add ops ~2x, reduces memory movement, and often gives near 2x throughput improvement for dense ops. But recall/accuracy tradeoff must be measured.

[16:05] Dr. Chen: I'm concerned about network egress if we go hosted. Our data residency / PHI-like constraints push us towards VPC/private or on-prem. Any perf delta between Redwood hosted vs private?
[16:20] Jordan: Hosting adds an additional network hop but our hosted service in the same cloud region typically keeps extra tail at <10ms if within same AZ; the main perf differences come from network isolation and whether you deploy on-prem with older hardware. For on-prem the variance can be higher depending on NICs and kernel tuning.
[16:45] Sofia: We also have strict egress cost policies — even 1M calls/day can be significant.
[16:52] Alex: For that reason, Dedicated or Private deployment (VPC peering or on-prem) can eliminate public egress fees; we can work through a hybrid model where embeddings compute is in your VPC and Redwood control plane stays managed.
[17:10] Ravi: If we do Private, are there differences in the batching/caching behavior?
[17:14] Maya: No, the runtime is the same. Configs (max-wait, batch size) are identical. The only difference is where kernels execute and network topology — which affects client-side latencies.

[18:50] Sofia: Talking about cost — what's the cost delta if we move from 768->384 and enable 8-bit quant on rerank? Ballpark per-1k queries numbers?
[19:05] Jordan: Rough ballpark: baseline (768, FP16, batching conservative) might be $0.45 per 1k rerank calls. Move to 384 + 8-bit + batching tuned you could be ~$0.15–0.2 per 1k. These are heuristics; we'll run a bench with your sample to show exact numbers.
[19:26] Ravi: Huge win if accuracy holds.

[21:00] Maya: On evaluation methodology — we'll run a 10k query bench with your labeled rerank set, sweep batch sizes [1,4,8,16,32], quant levels [fp16,8bit,4bit], and dims [384,768] where feasible. We'll report latency distribution (p50/p95/p99), throughput, GPU util, and cost per 1k.
[21:25] Dr. Chen: Can you also include KV-cache sim with hit-rates [5,15,25,40]?
[21:31] Maya: Absolutely. We'll show cost delta vs hit-rate and recommend TTLs.

[23:10] Sofia: For on-prem, we run NVIDIA H100s but only PCIe Gen4 interconnects; any kernel support concerns?
[23:20] Jordan: H100 PCIe is fine. The important part is software kernel selection — some quant kernels require new libs. We'll validate kernel compatibility in the bench. If needed we can provide a small shim or container with pegged kernels.

[25:40] Ravi: A question about fallbacks — if we miss capacity, can Redwood automatically route to a cheaper smaller model or degrade gracefully?
[25:54] Alex: Yes — smart routing with fallback policies is supported. You can set a policy: primary model (cross-encoder) with canary fallback to a cheaper bi-encoder hybrid that does re-rerank heuristics. We log A/B differences on responses so you can watch quality regressions.
[26:18] Ravi: Any way to estimate the quality drop with fallback?
[26:22] Maya: We can run a simulated fallback on your labeled data to estimate nDCG and precision impact.

[28:00] Dr. Chen: On security — what about KMS & audit logs when on-prem? We need HSM integration and enterprise key custody.
[28:12] Jordan: For Private we support customer-managed KMS and can integrate with HSM via PKCS#11 in on-prem deployments. Audit logs are shipped to your SIEM via collector; retention levels configurable. We'll send the security brief.

[30:00] Alex: Quick note on multi-tenant vs dedicated pools — if you want predictable p95 you should consider Dedicated GPUs. Shared hosted can have jitter spikes during noisy neighbors.
[30:12] Sofia: How much reserved capacity should we commit? We have variable traffic — seasonal spikes.
[30:18] Alex: We recommend a baseline reserved capacity sized for p95 on your 95th percentile traffic with burst capacity for peak windows. We'll help with sizing after the benchmark.

[32:50] Maya: A couple of rough numbers from internal infra: continuous batching with adaptive max-wait (5–10ms) and batching target 16 yields about 2.8x throughput improvement on transformers, p95 within SLO in most cases. Quantization to 8-bit nets an additional ~1.4x speedup on supported kernels. Combined can hit 4x effective ops.
[33:20] Ravi: Do you have a public benchmarking sheet?
[33:23] Alex: We'll share a benchmark spreadsheet and the runbook. Expect the Redwood bench to include raw logs and configs.

[35:40] Sofia: On the operational side, if we run on-prem, what telemetry do we get?
[35:46] Jordan: Full telemetry: per-route latency, model-level token counts, per-token cost estimators, and KV-cache hit/miss metrics. Dashboards can be hosted either on Redwood console or forwarded into Grafana in your VPC.

[37:10] Dr. Chen: We need a compliance pack (SOC2 evidence) and IP agreements if we run a PoC.
[37:20] Alex: We'll attach SOC2, data flow diagrams, and a PoC contract template to the follow-up email.

[39:00] Ravi: One last technical nit — vector storage. If we keep 768 dims can we use product quantization to compress document vectors on disk while serving dense ops uncompressed in GPU?
[39:12] Maya: Yes — hybrid: store compressed vectors in Lucene/FAISS with PQ, then for top-N do a partial re-rank on GPU with full-res vectors for accuracy. That reduces disk/IO cost and keeps GPU compute accurate.

[41:20] Sofia: Can Redwood's runtime pull compressed vectors and do dequant on the fly?
[41:26] Jordan: Yes, we support a flow where FAISS returns candidate ids, then a fetcher pulls full-res or dequantized embeddings into memory for rerank. There's a latency cost to that fetch; we can model it in the bench.

[43:00] Maya: Ok, quick recap of deliverables: 10k query bench, batch/quant/dim sweep, KV-cache hit-rate sim, cost-per-1k report, security brief, PoC contract.
[43:15] Dr. Chen: Sounds good. Prefer the bench week of 10/6 or 10/7.
[43:20] Alex: We'll target results by 10/09 and sync the PoC kick-off for 10/15 if numbers look good.

[45:00] Ravi: Any blockers on samples? We will upload 10k labeled queries to the shared S3 bucket — Sofia will provision access.
[45:08] Sofia: Yes, I'll send creds and sample logs by EOD 10/03.

[46:40] Maya: One more thing — for the bench we need GPU types and baseline latency numbers. You said H100 on-prem; if you want us to simulate hosted A100 vs your H100 we'll include both.
[46:55] Dr. Chen: Include both please.

[48:20] Alex: Great. Any other questions?
[48:28] Ravi: Not from me.
[48:30] Sofia: Nada.
[48:32] Dr. Chen: No.

[49:00] Alex: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with the plan + spreadsheet + security pack. Next meeting will be bench review.
